British Politics. The system of government and political activity in the United Kingdom, characterized by parliamentary democracy, constitutional monarchy, and party competition. From the nineteenth century onward, British politics became the model for liberal democracy in the English-speaking world, with expanding suffrage, cabinet government, and competing party ideologies. The political evolution of Britain from aristocratic oligarchy to mass democracy shaped not only the nation but influenced democratic movements globally.

The Glorious Revolution in sixteen eighty-eight and its subsequent settlement established parliamentary supremacy over the monarchy, creating the foundation for constitutional democracy. Centuries later, the Great Reform Act in eighteen thirty-two expanded voting rights and redistributed electoral representation, establishing a pattern of incremental democratic expansion throughout the nineteenth century.

The Liberal and Conservative parties emerged as the dominant competing forces in British politics. Ideological shifts between free trade liberalism and protective conservatism defined nineteenth-century politics. Women's suffrage became a major political battleground. Emmeline Pankhurst and the suffragettes waged a campaign of civil disobedience that ultimately succeeded in nineteen twenty-eight, when women over age twenty-one gained the right to vote.

The rise of the Labour Party in the early twentieth century fundamentally altered British politics. The Labour Party represented working-class interests and challenged the Liberal-Conservative duopoly that had dominated for over a century. British politics adapted to decolonization, the welfare state, and managed economic decline in the post-World War Two era. Tensions between social democracy and market liberalism persist in British political life today.
